III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00728

Or, in another form: “Our cause is the truth, and the truth of truth (haqq al-haqq). It is the outward meaning, and the inner meaning of the outward meaning (batin al-zahir), and the inner meaning of the inner meaning (batin al-batin). It is a secret, the secret of something still concealed, a secret hidden by another secret.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00729
We should also reflect on these lines attributed to the Fourth Imam, Ali Zayn al-Abidin (d. 95 AH/714 CE):
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00730

I hide the jewels of my knowledge, For fear that an ignorant man, seeing the truth, would crush us. Lord, if I revealed a single pearl of what I know, They would say, “So you worship idols!” And some Muslims would believe it lawful to shed my blood. They condemn as monstrous the most beautiful thing shown to them.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00731

Whether the Imam himself spoke these words or Shiite tradition later placed them in his mouth, they offer unmistakable evidence of how that tradition understands Shiism's inner teaching and the struggle to preserve it.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00732

This is why the discipline of taqiya—the duty to keep certain teachings private—is so strict. As we saw earlier, it follows directly from the idea of a truth entrusted to someone's care. Imam Ja'far goes so far as to say: “Whoever does not practise taqiya”—whether through carelessness or rejection of the inner teaching—“has no religion.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00733

In the Book of Shiite Beliefs (Kitab al-itiqadat), the great Shiite theologian Ibn Babuyeh (d. 381 AH/991 CE) writes: “The duty of taqiya must not be set aside until the Imam who announces the resurrection (al-Imam al-Qa'im) appears. Through him, religion (din) will be revealed in its entirety, so that from East to West it will be one and the same religion, as it was in the time of Adam.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00734

This already answers those who deny that Shiism has an inner teaching. If, as some have claimed and still claim, the Imams taught nothing beyond explanations of religious law (sharia) and ritual, the command to keep their teaching secret would make no sense. Haydar Amoli points out that these are precisely the things one may—and should—proclaim openly from mosque pulpits. Clearly, they cannot be what the Imams mean in the sayings quoted above.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00735

In his second conversation with Komayl, the First Imam divided humanity into three groups. Several sayings of the Sixth Imam make the same distinction: “We, the Imams, are the sages who teach; our Shiites are those whom we initiate; everyone else is foam carried along by the flood.” There are therefore three groups. The first consists of the divine sages, the alim rabbani, those who fully embody divine wisdom. Strictly speaking, the title belongs to the Imams, though it can also be extended to sages who have become like them.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00736
The second group consists of believers “whose hearts have been tested,” who receive and pass on this teaching.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00737

Finally comes the great mass—not simply people who have not been initiated, but those who deny or stubbornly reject the very possibility of spiritual knowledge. Imam Ja'far expressly says that there is no fourth group.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00738

Haydar Amoli's generous attempt to bring Shiites and Sufis together, and to help both understand who they are and what they owe to one another, follows naturally from this distinction. Everyone must decide where they belong. Those who call themselves Shiites but deny the Imams' inner teaching because they cannot bear even the idea of it, and those Sufis who practise a spiritual path while ignoring its source and foundation, cannot claim to belong to the second group, much less the first.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00739

The second group is made up of believers whose hearts have been tested: people who accept the full weight and consequences of the threefold profession of faith (shahadat). Openly or unseen, they keep God's testimony alive on earth. Through them, this remains a world that God looks upon—a world that still matters to God. Among them is a smaller circle entrusted especially with passing on the Imams' secrets and keeping them alive in the hearts of tested believers. Of these the First Imam said: “Where are they? How many are there? I swear by God, they are very few, but their standing is exceedingly high.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00740

This circle forms a hidden spiritual hierarchy, an idea fundamental to Twelver Shiism. In Corbin's account, non-Shiite Sufism probably borrowed it from Shiism, because the hierarchy's very existence, structure, and continuity depend on a permanent spiritual centre: the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam. Unless we understand this unseen community, we cannot understand the nature or stakes of Shiism's spiritual struggle. It also changes the way we understand the relationship between Shiism and Sufism. More than that, it shows how the Shiism of the Twelve Imams can offer its spiritual message quietly amid the turmoil of our world: not by compromising with a supposedly unstoppable course of historical change, but by bearing witness to another world and reminding us that such a world exists.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
en-book-1-ch-3-s4
4. The Invisible Spiritual Hierarchies
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00741

From one generation to the next, a small number of chosen people pass on a task that remains unknown to almost everyone. It is not the kind of work that appears in official reports or can be uncovered by a social survey. These people form spiritual hierarchies mentioned in certain traditions whose origins and precise meaning remain somewhat mysterious.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00742

Around them gather those who are Shiites in the fullest sense: people who receive their teaching and share their task. They belong to the second of the three groups described by the Imams, the believers “whose hearts God has tested through faith.” They have the strength to uphold the Imams' cause, however difficult, in a world that may know nothing of it.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00743

This teaching is so central to Shiism that the Shaykhi school, as we shall see in Book VI, gives it a particularly far-reaching interpretation. Seeking to preserve or restore the complete teaching of the holy Imams, the Shaykhis present it as the fourth pillar of Shiite doctrine. The first is God's oneness (tawhid); the second concerns prophecy; the third, the Imams and their spiritual role; and the fourth, the Shiite community itself, understood in a deeper sense.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00744

We can best describe it using a familiar Western expression: an Ecclesia spiritualis, a spiritual community. Its hierarchy is invisible and its members remain unknown. Their place within it depends entirely on their inner spiritual qualities.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00745

Our authors see this hierarchy as something borne out by experience. Some people, after all, are more spiritually developed than others, nearer to God, or further advanced in knowledge, spiritual awareness, and devotion. A hierarchy of different degrees therefore exists among them. Such outstanding individuals were present even in the time of the Imams and have continued to appear since: Salman the Persian, Abu Dharr, the two men named Jabir, Mufazzal, and the four successive deputies (na'ib) of the Hidden Imam during the “Lesser Occultation,” the first period of his concealment.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00746

Shiites recognise such figures as intermediaries and guides acting on the Imam's behalf. Even during the “Greater Occultation,” the period in which we now live, they may be granted access to the Imam's presence. Such meetings involve a way of perceiving that goes beyond the physical senses.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00747

But observing that some people possess greater spiritual gifts does not explain why this hierarchy exists. Its deeper structure follows the order in which beings come forth from the Muhammadan Reality (Haqiqat muhammadiya), the primordial reality first brought into existence, which we have already discussed at length and will return to below. This reality reaches its complete expression in the company of the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones.” The final figure in that company, considered in the order in which divine realities become manifest, is the Twelfth Imam, now hidden. Our entire work will end by returning to him (Book VII).
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00748

For now, the essential point is that every part of these spiritual hierarchies—their purpose, their structure, their way of existing, and the way they act—centres on the Twelfth Imam and his unseen presence. He is the “pole of poles,” their central support and the key to understanding them. This is also connected with the great spiritual cycles: the cycle of walayat, the Imams' spiritual guidance, following the cycle of prophecy (see Chapter V and Book VII). The relationship between the unseen hierarchies and the Twelfth Imam is so complex that it would require a book of its own. Here I can give only the briefest outline.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00749

In some sayings of the Imams, the hierarchies appear in a simpler form than in later traditions. Imam Ja'far, foretelling the inevitable concealment (ghaybat) of the Imamate, speaks of thirty chosen companions, the Nuqaba, or spiritual leaders. Across the generations of the Greater Occultation, which began in 329 AH/940 CE, they enjoy the privilege of meeting and keeping company with the Hidden Imam. During the Lesser Occultation (874–940 CE), the most spiritually advanced Shiites could still gain access to him. Since the Greater Occultation, this privilege belongs only to the thirty Nuqaba.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00750

Their meetings raise a question: where does the Hidden Imam live? The traditions sometimes speak of the mysterious valley of Shamrikh near Yemen and sometimes of the mystical city of Hurqalya. In either case, the setting belongs to a hidden spiritual region called the “eighth climate.” The mysterious Green Island, visited by a pilgrim whose story survives in Shiite tradition, belongs to this same region (see Book VII).
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00751

This is the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world: a subtler counterpart of the world we perceive with our senses. It stands between our physical world and the purely spiritual world, which is entirely separate from it. Through this imaginal world, the Imam can be present to our world while remaining invisible to its inhabitants. His thirty chosen companions exist and act in a similar way. They too are hidden from human eyes.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00752

Hence their name, rijal al-ghayb: the people of the unseen world, the hidden ones, the Invisibles. Their number never changes. When one dies—or, more exactly, when that person's presence in this world finally ends—another takes the vacant place. They are therefore also called Abdal, those who replace one another. Elsewhere, I have tried to show why the imaginal world is indispensable for understanding the spiritual life we are studying here.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00753

Another text from roughly the same period, written by a disciple of Imam Ja'far, calls these spiritual figures Abdal by name. It is a prayer composed by Dawud, a grandson of the Second Imam, Hasan Mujtaba, and a companion of the Fifth and Sixth Imams. The Shiite religious calendar recommends reciting it on the fifteenth day of Rajab, the seventh month of the lunar year. In practice, it is better known through Dawud's mother, under the title “the devotional practice of the mother of Dawud” (amal Umm Dawud).
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00754

It is an especially beautiful prayer, embracing the whole family of sacred history. It sends greetings in turn to the three great archangels, those who support God's Throne, the guardian angels, Adam and Eve, Abel and Seth, every prophet named in the biblical and Arab traditions, Jesus and his twelve Imams (from Simon to George), the Prophet Muhammad and his twelve Imams, the Abdal and the Awtad, the members of every family descended from the Imams, and all devout people. It ends: “Honour, my God, all those angels and prophets whom I have named, and all those whom I have not named.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00755

An even earlier text, a saying attributed to the Fourth Imam, Ali Zayn al-Abidin, already describes different ranks within the spiritual hierarchy. In a conversation with Jabir ibn Yazid al-Jufi, the Imam names seven matters that a faithful Shiite must know through spiritual understanding (marifat): the meaning of the profession of God's oneness; the meanings of God's Names and Attributes; the prophets, who are the abwab, or doorways between God and humanity; the Twelve Imams; the “Supports” or “Pillars” (Arkan); the Nuqaba; and the Nujaba (see also p. 198 below).
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00756
Below the Imam, this gives us three ranks:
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00757

The four Supports (Arkan). These are four figures who remain the same through every age, with no replacements. They are generally identified with the prophets taken from this world by God without passing through death: Enoch (also identified with Idris or Hermes), Elijah, Khidr, and Jesus. They live on without dying, sustained by the continuing presence of their spiritual centre, the Imam.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00758
The thirty Nuqaba. These are the spiritual leaders already mentioned.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00759
The forty Nujaba. These are the spiritually noble ones.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00760

The last two groups together number seventy. Their numbers remain fixed, but new members take the places of those who leave this world. Both their numbers and their duties are connected with the idea of God's Names descending through the different levels of being, each Name presiding over a particular universe. This is a very complex body of spiritual thought, which we cannot examine in detail here (see Books III and VI below).
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00761
Shiite theologians also know of teachers who place a further, constantly renewed group below the Nujaba: 360 righteous and wise people, corresponding in number to the degrees of the heavenly sphere.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00762

Yet the clearest statements attributed to the Imams themselves do not seem to mention this additional group. Other differences exist as well. In a conversation with Mufazzal al-Jufi, for example, Imam Ja'far explains the hierarchy in detail. Every Imam, in every age, is accompanied by forty chosen spiritual companions: twenty-eight Nujaba and twelve Nuqaba, including the Abdal and the Awtad. Their total, forty, matches the number elsewhere assigned to the Nujaba alone.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00763

These early teachings attributed to the Imams help us understand the more elaborate versions found elsewhere. An Ismaili account, for example, says: “Our masters have declared: out of humanity we chose four thousand; out of those four thousand, four hundred; out of those four hundred, forty; out of those forty, four; and out of those four, one alone, who is the pole (qotb). The stability of the world rests upon him. The world cannot exist without him for a single instant; without him it could not continue to exist.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00764

Another version says: “God has on earth three hundred distinguished people (a'yan)”—the Arabic word can mean both “eyes” and people as precious as one's own eyes. They are the eyes through which, in Ruzbihan's words, ours remains a world that God looks upon.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00765

The account continues: “Three hundred whose hearts correspond to Adam's heart”—the Nuqaba, or spiritual guides—“forty whose hearts correspond to Moses' heart”—the Nujaba—“seven whose hearts correspond to Abraham's heart”—the seven Abdal—“four whose hearts correspond to the archangel Gabriel's heart”—the Awtad, or pillars—“three whose hearts correspond to the archangel Michael's heart”—the three Afrad—“and one whose heart corresponds to the archangel Seraphiel's heart, the pole of poles (qotb al-aqtab).”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00766
This one supreme example of “seraphic” humanity is always the Imam—in our own time, the Hidden Imam.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00767

We will find the same pattern in Ruzbihan (Book III), though the order of the Nuqaba and Nujaba is reversed. To trace the full development of these hierarchies, we would then need to follow them through the work of Ibn Arabi and his many commentators.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00768

The numbers here must, of course, be understood as symbols. They express relationships within the cosmos and the rhythm by which the different levels of existence are ordered (tartib al-wujud). Still, Shiite authors—especially the Shaykhis—tend to retain three ranks, like a three-part entrance (rawaq) leading to the threshold of the Imam: the four Supports (Arkan), the thirty Nuqaba, and the forty Nujaba, as named in the saying of the Fourth Imam.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00769

That is why the thirty Nuqaba may be identified with the Awtad, the “tent pegs” that hold up the earthly world or the cosmic tent; with the Abdal, who replace one another; and with subordinate spiritual “poles,” since they carry the Imam's gifts to other people. They are also the rijal al-ghayb, the people of the unseen, or Invisibles. Entirely pure and devoted to divine service, they are kept hidden by God from the eyes of oppressors until the Last Day (Yawm al-Din).
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00770

The idea of this hidden spiritual hierarchy is so deeply bound up with Shiite thought that, when we encounter it elsewhere—for instance, in Sufi texts outside Shiism—we can recognise an understanding of the Imams that has been carried over into Sufism without openly identifying itself as such. This may have escaped attention until now because Shiite sources have been so widely neglected.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00771

For our purposes, what matters most is how Shiism—and particularly the Shaykhi school—has understood these hierarchies by taking the concealment (ghaybat) of the Imam seriously and following the idea through to its consequences. In this reading, Shiism stands as a defence against every attempt to turn spiritual life into a social institution, to confuse it with social organisation, or to make compromises that threaten its independent reality and its priority over worldly concerns.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00772

The Hidden Imam ordered his last appointed deputy (na'ib) not to name a successor. From then on, the Imams' followers would look to sages who preserved and passed on their teaching, among whom the members of the hidden spiritual hierarchies could be found, though without being publicly known. When Ali al-Samarri, the last deputy personally appointed by the Hidden Imam, died in 329 AH/940 CE, the Greater Occultation began. His final words were: “From now on, the matter belongs to God.” Those words express the whole spirit of Shiism. From then on, the Hidden Imam became the central figure in Shiite religious awareness. The history of that awareness is, in a sense, the history of his unseen presence (see Book VII).
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00773

Accordingly, when the Shaykhis discuss the sages who carry this teaching forward, they stress that the Imam directed his followers towards the existence of a kind of person. He did not identify particular individuals by name. This is no church hierarchy. Its members are distinguished only by their inner spiritual worth and the degree of their closeness to the Imam. Who they are remains the Imam's secret. No member can therefore publicly announce that they belong to it or be identified by outward signs.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00774

We might apply to each of them the rule that governs the knights of the Grail: “His strength is sacred so long as he remains unknown to all.” They are hidden from ordinary sight for the very reason that the Imam is hidden. Above all, the Imam is concealed today because human beings have concealed him from themselves.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00775

Human awareness has become unable to know or recognise him, to perceive how he exists and acts, or to recognise the “place” in which he dwells. The same inability hides those who are, as it were, members of his own being and who together make up his very Name. His final appearance will not be some outside event suddenly imposed on the world. It will mark the completion of a transformation in human consciousness.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00776
A beautiful passage by Muhammad Karim Khan Kirmani (d. 1288 AH/1870 CE) brings the point together:
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00777

When you have reflected in the way I have explained, you will understand why it is not possible today to know who the Nuqaba and Nujaba are. We are not permitted to ask for their individual names or identities. Nor are they permitted to answer. For they are the sacred Name of the Imam of this age, and during the time of his concealment (ghaybat) his name must not be spoken. Many sayings forbid the mention of their names.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00778

They are the Hidden Imam's real and living Name because a person's name expresses what that person is. What a person is can be understood as their light, and that light as the radiance they give out. The Imam's radiance is his Shiites (shia-ye u), his followers. It is therefore wrong to name these people or seek to discover who they are.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00779

Through a special act of divine kindness, someone may happen to recognise one of them. That person was capable of receiving such knowledge, and God granted it. If God does not make them known to someone else, that person plainly lacks this capacity and has no right to demand it. Yes, this is God's clear and deliberate arrangement for our time: people should recognise that this whole category of persons—the Nuqaba and the Nujaba—exists, acknowledge their role, and feel a bond of solidarity with them.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00780

In the same way, we know that there is a Hidden Imam (Imam gha'ib). We must acknowledge his existence and his spiritual role and remain in communion with him, even though we do not know him in his physical person.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00781

This passage is characteristic of a form of Shiite spirituality shaped by the idea of the Hidden Imam, with all that this idea can mean to a mature religious consciousness. There is nothing here resembling a Church, with its clergy and its authority to decide doctrine. Nor does it resemble certain modern “esoteric” organisations that claim an unbroken line of spiritual succession (successio apostolica) and appeal to mysterious documents as proof of their official legitimacy. Above all, there is nothing that allows religious reality to be confused with a social system—a confusion whose painful consequences we have seen in the testimony of a Sunni Muslim.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00782

The standing of these spiritual hierarchies is perfectly expressed in a sacred saying (hadith qudsi): “My Friends (Awliya'i) dwell beneath my tabernacles; no one knows them except me.” When one of these people passes from earthly life into another life, someone else takes that person's place.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00783

But this succession remains the Imam's secret. From a Shaykhi perspective, we could say that nothing is more deeply hidden than the structure of the Shiite community. And nothing offers a stronger defence against attempts to subject divine reality (res divina) to worldly ambitions and the desire for power.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00784

At the same time, because this hidden teaching looks towards the final fulfilment of history, it also works against every attempt to freeze religion into fixed doctrines. The final age began when the mission of the “last prophet” came to its close. It will not end until the final Imam appears. He will lift every veil from the secrets that God's Friends have spent this cycle of spiritual guidance (da'irat al-walayat) and concealment helping receptive souls to understand. Ultimately, they are awakening those who can grasp the meaning of the trust that Adam agreed to carry.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00785

To follow Adam in his turning back to God, his “repentance,” and to accept the threefold profession of faith (shahadat) is to reverse the movement of Adam's “descent from paradise.” It means taking part in a spiritual struggle against the urge to rush blindly forward. Today that urge has many names. It likes to call itself “irreversible,” all the more insistently because it does not really know where its supposed “progress” is taking it.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00786
Of course, Shiite spiritual philosophy, like other traditional paths of divine wisdom, has never ignored the idea of an “evolution” embracing every form of life and the whole history of humanity.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00787

But here the movement goes by another name, because its direction is understood in terms of both its source and its goal. It belongs to a history beyond ordinary history—a metahistory. Without such a dimension, talk of the “meaning of history” is only a metaphor. One principle governs these Shiite thinkers, and others as well: “Nothing rises to heaven except what has come down from heaven.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00788

The only human beginning we can truly imagine is one that corresponds to our understanding of the end. In other words, the story we tell about our origins is inseparable from what we believe human life is ultimately for. That remains true today.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00789

But unlike the prevailing ideas of our time, the sacred history of humanity and the world is, in this traditional understanding, cyclical. It has an arc of descent (nuzul) and an arc of return or ascent (su'ud). Its direction is vertical—like the soaring lines of Gothic architecture. It is not the story of a supposedly irreversible, straight-line advance from an unimaginably distant past, based on the unsupported assumption that humanity must have begun at a level lower than its own present state. It is a story of gradually turning back, returning, and rising towards what the original descent placed beyond our reach. Here I refer readers to the beautiful pages by Muhammad Karim Khan Kirmani, translated elsewhere, on the meaning of this “world in ascent.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
en-book-1-ch-3-s5
5. What Is at Stake in Shiism's Spiritual Struggle—and Why It Still Matters
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00790
By now, I hope, what is at stake has become clear. We can look at the question in two ways. The first concerns what Shiism is in itself and where it stands within Islam.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00791
The second concerns the spiritual and religious condition of our time as a whole. In drawing these threads together, I am returning to the concerns raised in Chapter I of this book.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00792

The first question takes us back to the Shiite spiritual figures discussed at the beginning of this chapter. Haydar Amoli, a thinker of exceptional quality, analysed their position in the eighth Islamic century (the fourteenth century CE). As I have noted, his account continued to apply in later periods and has lost none of its relevance in our own time.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00793

The sayings of the holy Imams quoted here, together with those still to come, make one thing clear: a form of Shiism that wished to be nothing more than an outward religion of law (sharia) would contradict its own nature. It would cut away an essential part of the Imams' teaching. When the Imams speak of the “secret” entrusted to those capable of bearing it, they are speaking of gnosis: direct spiritual knowledge. Shiite teaching is, in a distinctive sense, the spiritual knowledge at the heart of Islam. Shiism itself is the continuous line through which that knowledge is passed on (silsilat al-irfan).
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00794

That is enough to settle the dispute between the divine sages and mystics (hukama rabbaniya and urafa) on one side, and those who would reduce Shiism to the legal rules taught by religious jurists (fuqaha) on the other. The “difficult cause,” the burden that the Imams place on believers whose hearts have been tested, is contained in the three parts of the profession of faith (shahadat). The recognition that God is one is inseparable from acknowledging the prophetic message. In the same way, acknowledging the Prophet's message loses its force if one does not also acknowledge the Imams as its inner meaning and spiritual continuation.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00795
An inner meaning cannot exist on its own, entirely detached from the outward form that gives it expression.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00796

But the reverse is just as true. Strip an outward religious form of its inner meaning—of its power to point beyond itself towards another reality—and it becomes a lifeless body, an empty shell. We have heard the Imams insist that without this deeper meaning the Qur'an would long ago have become a dead book. Revelation would be reduced to a museum of theological curiosities, which is precisely how it already appears to someone who rejects the possibility of religious knowledge.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00797

For a long time, people have tended to see Islam only through its Sunni majority. When they contrast a religion centred on religious law with a spiritual path that crosses the threshold into invisible worlds, they naturally turn to Sufism.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00798

But the relationship between Shiism and Sufism has received very little attention. When it has been discussed, the two have generally been described as incompatible. Is that not a hasty judgment, born of unfamiliarity with Shiite spirituality? Reading the words of the Imams forces us to reconsider the whole question. That is what Haydar Amoli, a Shiite thinker of the fourteenth century, had already done (see also Book IV, Chapter I).
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00799

The passages we have studied help explain why Amoli can make this seemingly startling claim without intending a paradox: “The Sufis are those who deserve to be called Shiites in the true sense (al-shia al-haqiqiya), and believers whose hearts have been tested (mu'min mumtahan).” Later Shiite Sufis would repeat his statement. The reverse seems to follow: if true Shiites are Sufis, then those Shiites who reject Sufism can be called Shiites only in a figurative sense (majazi). Perhaps.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00800
But what exactly does it mean to reject Sufism?
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00801

Here we immediately think of a kind of Shiite spiritual teacher already mentioned, and to whom we will return. These mystics practise the kind of spirituality associated with Sufism and use its language, yet belong to none of the Sufi orders. Some even have serious reservations about them. We have already noted several reasons: the excessive importance sometimes attached to the personality of the Sufi master, despite the inevitable limits of any individual; certain practices; and certain theories about the nature of being which, when poorly understood by followers, can encourage moral carelessness or self-indulgence.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00802

There is no doubt that some Shiite mystics belong among the believers “whose hearts have been tested,” the second group named by the Imams, while not being Sufis in the usual sense. Haydar Amoli's claim must therefore have a far wider meaning than it first appears to have. Otherwise, we would be driven into a still stranger paradox. Was he including Sunni Sufis as Shiites without their knowing it—even though many had fiercely attacked Shiism? Was he trying to bring back these “lost children” of Shiism, as his life's work seems to suggest?
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00803

I think a basic principle of spiritual life can help us understand the problem. What distinguishes Sufi Islam from an Islam centred on religious law is that it is a religion of divine love. As we noted earlier (pp. 81 onward and 101 onward), this raises a formidable theological question: how can we speak of love, or even use the word, while remaining faithful to the absolute oneness of God (tawhid)? We shall see in Book III how painfully Ruzbihan wrestled with this question in both his thought and his life.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00804

But something that has rarely been recognised is obvious to anyone who has lived Shiite spirituality from within: Shiism, as a religion of walayat, the Imams' bond of spiritual closeness and guidance, is itself the religion of love in Islam, in a particularly full and essential sense. At the deepest level of divine being—the divine Ground (Kuhh al-dhat, comparable to Meister Eckhart's Grund)—God is so far beyond human reach that the idea of a mutual relationship of love seems impossible.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00805

But love can turn with confidence towards the figures through whom God becomes manifest, the forms of the revealed God (Deus revelatus). Those figures are precisely the eternal spiritual realities of the Imams, in whom the divine Names and Attributes are made present (see Chapter VII below).
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00806

That is why the threefold profession of faith matters so much in practice. From the beginning, it makes Shiism both a guide and a foundation for the longings that find expression in Sufism. At the same time, Shiism's understanding of the Imams protects those longings from going astray, particularly from the dizzying temptation to identify oneself with God as God remains beyond revelation.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00807

This is why Haydar Amoli and thinkers like him are not troubled by the observation that most Sufis are Sunni Muslims—to such an extent that many people instinctively associate Sufism with Sunni Islam. In his view, the presence of Sufism within Sunni Islam answers a need that does not arise in the same way within Shiism. He is also keenly aware of the spiritual dangers Sufism has faced in a Sunni setting, where its deepest aspirations have been separated from both their roots and their fulfilment.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00808

This leads us to a central idea in Shiite spirituality, one that reaches beyond the familiar opposition between the Islam of the legal scholars and the Islam of the Sufis. I have already put it this way: Twelver Shiism, when lived in its entirety, is already a spiritual path, a tariqat. The Shiite believer “whose heart has been tested through faith” is already, in that broad sense, a Sufi, without needing to join a Sufi order. Such a person is already a “Shiite in the true sense.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00809

But here the word Sufi reaches beyond its usual meaning. We should translate it instead as “mystic” and recognise that Shiite Islam has great mystics who are not necessarily Sufis in the narrower, organised sense.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00810

Take Muhammad Baqir Majlisi, the great theologian of Safavid Shiism to whom we owe a monumental collection of Shiite sayings. He objected strongly when people called his father, Muhammad Taqi Majlisi (d. 1660), a “Sufi.” He was not entirely wrong. His father was not a Sufi in the narrower meaning of the term, yet he was unquestionably a genuine mystic. This is more than a fine point of wording. Understanding the distinction matters if we want to find our way through Shiite spiritual life.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00811

The conclusion, then, is that a Shiite who lives the faith fully, a believer “whose heart has been tested,” must personally follow the spiritual way (tariqat) of the Twelve Imams. Such a person's spiritual life encompasses much of what people in the West generally call Sufism, without necessarily sharing the weaknesses that have exposed some Sufi practices, organisations, and forms of expression to criticism from Shiite spiritual teachers—even in the time of the Imams themselves.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00812

At the same time, the Imams' teaching, lived as a personal reality and guarded as a sacred trust, already protects the Shiite seeker from another danger: a rigid, merely literal religion. Such literalism strips outward forms of the inner meaning that gives them life, cuts them off from the spiritual worlds to which they point, and finally opens the way to confusing religion with society. Reject the Imams' secret, which is itself the spiritual path of Islam, and little remains beyond the rites of a social religion. Then a form of scholarship that has itself become secular will explain and justify those rites solely by the role they play in society.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00813

And so we return to where we began: the troubling question raised by the Jordanian participant whose testimony I described earlier. In our study group in Tehran, we had asked: “Is there no way out? What answer could a Shiite give?” The answer, I believe, is already contained in the First Imam's conversations with Komayl ibn Ziyad, as well as in the many other sayings of the Imams we have examined—and could easily have multiplied.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00814

But consider those who reject haqiqat: the inner truth whose meanings rise beyond the outward words and appearances, through one spiritual world after another, and thereby give this visible world its meaning. The worlds are joined by an axis leading to their heavenly centre. Those who dismiss these inner meanings will also dismiss the idea of a purely spiritual community held together by that truth, invisible yet real. What happens to such people when the outward order of a traditional society begins to fall apart? Because they have identified religion with that social order, their very understanding of religion falls with it.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00815

That is the grave question facing us today: is there still, hidden within Islam, a spiritual strength capable of carrying forward the future of a purely spiritual Islam? For Shiism, answering that question should simply mean answering the Imams' continual call. Its threefold profession of faith gives it a calling to show, through its very existence, that Islam is more than the outward letter of religious law (sharia), just as social life is not identical with religious reality.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00816

This is the final choice posed by Shiism's “spiritual struggle.” One path is surrender: spiritual life is absorbed into social structures, drawn into the ambitions of those who seek power, and made to serve authorities that either have no idea what “spiritual” means or destroy its meaning all the more effectively because they once understood it. For the person who can truly profane or blaspheme is not the unbeliever, but the believer.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00817

The other path is faith in the divine incognito—God's hidden presence—even in what we might call desperado fiducialis, a despair that still holds fast to trust. It is faith in a divine hiddenness that persists as a challenge and finds its clearest expression in the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam. Here religious reality cannot be turned into an object, forced into an objective system, or absorbed into social or collective life (see Book VII). A believer inspired by such faith will find a way to resolve the problems that arise today from remaining faithful to the requirements of religious law. That believer's spiritual struggle will end in victory.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00818

It is significant that two expressions familiar from certain Western spiritual traditions—the divine incognito and the Ecclesia spiritualis, the spiritual community—should help us convey Shiism's message. They also bring us to the second way of considering our subject, which I proposed at the start of this section. Their distance from the major intellectual fashions of our day tells us something about the unprecedented crisis affecting Christian theology in the West.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00819

After twenty centuries of Christianity, we can now hear Christian theologians denouncing what they call a confusion between Christianity and “systems of religious redemption.” They say these other systems take human beings out of this world and its history, open a window onto a world beyond that can explain this one, and show a path towards recovering a lost human nature. They claim to find in the Bible something that twenty centuries of Christianity had never thought to look for there. They present it as a safeguard against faith becoming what they now call an “escape to heaven.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00820

For such thinkers, the question is no longer how to defend belief by appealing to the limits of human power. Human capacities, they tell us, have no limits. The powers of homo progressivus, humanity in constant progress, are driving homo sapiens towards ever greater social organisation, collective systems, all-embracing control, and the absolute rule of technical experts ... “How can we avoid killing God?” our Jordanian Muslim had asked in anguish. Some Christian theologians answer by going even further than Nietzsche's declaration. They claim that Christian faith is defined by a confrontation between triumphant human power and the helplessness of a Creator who has been overcome. This, apparently, would be the true revelation of God's transcendence.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00821
Perhaps this is indeed what a certain “demystifying” theological argument reveals.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00822

Yet it is striking how closely that argument agrees with the most radical rejection of religious knowledge. It would be so much simpler, and more candid, to say so. I ask only whether some Western readers might be willing to attempt an experiment: set the results of these dazzling exercises in post-Christian theology beside a direct reading of the Qur'an in Arabic, or beside a few of the Imams' sayings of the kind quoted in this book. Perhaps those who try will hear an inner summons as powerful as the voices of a Last Judgment ...
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00823

Anyone to whom such an experiment means nothing may find it perfectly natural to hear that belonging to the Prophet's religion is incompatible with life in a modern state, and that Islam is therefore doomed. Such people can imagine nothing except dragging Islam into the ruin they foresee for themselves.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00824
But believers “whose hearts have been tested” will surely turn the question around: what if the judgment falls the other way?
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00825

“How many are they? Where are they?” the Imam asked. Their identity remains God's secret. They are “very few,” but their existence is enough, because they will not be swept along by the flood—the flood that bears so many different names today. And the more of them there are, the less of the “foam carried by the flood” of which the Imam also spoke.
